You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test failure is due to commons-compress version 1.7 reading stored ZIP entries with null (NUL) bytes instead of the expected data bytes, while version 1.6 reads them correctly. 

The test `testReadingOfFirstStoredEntry` opens a ZIP file, reads the first entry, and asserts the size and content of the entry. The failure indicates the input stream produces unexpected NUL bytes.

Examining `ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry()`, this method reads and parses the ZIP entry header and sets up the input stream for reading the entry data. It reads various header fields including compression method, sizes, and file name. It handles entries with and without data descriptors differently. If a data descriptor is used, it defers reading size and CRC until it reads the data descriptor later.

`closeEntry()` ensures that the current entry's remaining data is fully read or skipped before moving to the next entry. It reads remaining bytes by calling `drainCurrentEntryData()` or skipping bytes. It also reads the data descriptor if used and resets the inflater for compressed entries.

`drainCurrentEntryData()` reads the remaining bytes of the current entry from the input stream to ensure the position is correct for the next entry.

`readDataDescriptor()` reads the trailing data descriptor metadata which contains the corrected CRC, compressed size, and size values when the sizes weren't known before. It checks for 4 or 8 byte sizes and sets these values on the entry.

The test symptom of getting NUL bytes indicates the stream providing the entry data is incorrectly positioned or the number of bytes read for the first stored entry is wrong in version 1.7. Inspecting `closeEntry()` shows that it attempts to align the stream if the data is not fully read and uses logic to push back certain bytes in case excess bytes were consumed due to compression streams.

The difference is likely related to the handling of the stored (i.e., uncompressed) entries with data descriptors. The pushback or remaining bytes logic may have changed in 1.7, causing some bytes of actual data to be skipped or replaced by zeros. This would result in corrupt data (NUL bytes) when reading the first entry.

Thus, the root cause is in the interaction of entry data reading, `closeEntry()` logic, and deferred setting of sizes due to data descriptors, causing the underlying stream to read incorrect bytes and yield invalid output. The logic in `closeEntry()` especially with pushback and skipping handling for stored entries with data descriptors looks likely to have introduced this regression.

Next, it would be useful to review related methods managing the input stream position and buffer management to verify this hypothesis, especially those called inside `closeEntry()` and when reading entry data.

org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry()
org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipArchiveInputStream.readDataDescriptor()
